entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gregory Thaumaturgus (c. 213 – c. 270 CE), also known as Gregory the Miracle-Worker and Gregory of Neocaesarea, stands as a pivotal figure in the early Christianization of Pontus, a Roman province in Asia Minor. He served as Bishop of Neocaesarea, capital of Pontus, during the mid-3rd century, a tumultuous period marked by Roman persecution and the nascent spread of Christianity beyond urban centers. His biographical details, notably his conversion from paganism, are primarily known through the hagiographic writings of Gregory of Nyssa and Eusebius of Caesarea, which emphasize his intellectual prowess and charismatic evangelism. His significance lies in his extraordinary success in converting a predominantly pagan region to Christianity, transforming a small community of seventeen believers into a vast Christian populace.

Born Theodorus in Neocaesarea to a wealthy pagan family, Gregory initially pursued rhetorical and legal studies. His intellectual journey led him to Caesarea Maritima, where he became a disciple of the celebrated Christian theologian Origen, spending five years (c. 233-238 CE) immersed in Christian philosophy and scripture. This period profoundly shaped his theological understanding, particularly his articulation of the Trinity, as evidenced in his 'Declaration of Faith' (Ekthesis pisteos). Returning to Pontus, he was appointed Bishop of Neocaesarea by Phaedimus, Bishop of Amasea, around 240 CE. His episcopacy was characterized by zealous missionary activity, including the destruction of pagan temples and the performance of numerous miracles, which earned him the epithet "Thaumaturgus" (miracle-worker) and were crucial to his evangelistic success among the local populace.
